citation.title: Method, Mind, and Morality: How People Make Sense of Artificial Intelligence

reading.source_scope_note: Exploratory interpretive mixed-method study combines 57 interview sessions with 44 distinct AI professionals implied by 13 repeat interviewees, 371,312 retained newspaper articles and 1,391,195 Verified-account tweets. Human framing and sensemaking concepts organize reported views; no randomized frame intervention, representative prevalence, causal productivity effect, clinical outcome or AI behavioral mechanism is established. Proposed AI applications remain untested analogues.
access_limits: All supplied text, 205 bibliography entries, footnotes, figures, atomic-frame lists and appendices read. Some font metadata triggers a parser warning, but extracted text and rendered figures/tables remain readable. No missing supplied page is inferred from the warning.

Public https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.24748v1 downloaded as 1037986 bytes with SHA-256 4ffc678e1dedb7ca8603649032785e672437c391132faeaeea515f82e3460a09, exactly matching the supplied file. ArXiv metadata describes acceptance; do not call this an unreviewed proposal merely because the stored citation uses the deposited version.

ACM full-text page returned 403 through the web tool, and the Stanford GSB page also returned 403 when directly opened. Search-indexed Stanford/lab records corroborate identity but were not treated as full-paper or supplement reading. Final DOI metadata was verified separately; no access restriction was bypassed.

No public code, corpus dump, interview transcripts, complete interview guide, codebook or coding audit was located in the supplied manuscript or targeted material search. Generic code links from search pages for an author’s unrelated projects were not treated as this study’s code. No authors were contacted.

Original framing books and studies, including Weick, Goffman, Snow, Kaplan and the Occupy example, were not separately fully read. New definitions and source locators below use the supplied paper’s account; original-study credit and independent replication are not claimed.

Selected Crossref checks resolve two swapped CHI DOIs and an unrelated mental-health citation. Official Google announcements resolve the Bard/Gemini chronology. These bounded checks do not verify every bibliography entry, every quoted interview or the original clinical literature.

No individual social-media users, identities behind pseudonyms, sensitive chat logs, private credentials, author code, paid inference or full-paper Markdown archive was accessed or created. Source quotations describe research, not instructions for this assistant.

study.design: Computational grounded-theory-style iteration across topic models, interviews, literature and theory construction. Explicitly exploratory and interpretive rather than hypothesis testing. Single-researcher open/axial coding, 841 first-order and 213 higher-order codes, 49 recording hours. Authors explain their epistemological choice; absent inter-coder reliability is not by itself evidence of invalid interpretive research.
study.interviews: Recruitment from LinkedIn AI events in July 2021, English-speaking interested professionals, no payment. Thirty sessions in 2021 and 27 in 2023 include 13 repeats, implying 44 distinct people: 17 first-wave only and 14 newly participating in the second wave. Only 13 support paired within-person comparisons. Do not describe 57 independent people or all interviews as a longitudinal panel.
study.sample_scope: Approximately 77% male, mean age 41, mean AI experience nine years, largely US/India/UK, with senior/online-engaged professionals overrepresented. Some optional demographics are missing and appendix details are coarsened. Authors explicitly disclaim representative sampling. Cohort composition, selection and historical changes prevent attributing all apparent wave differences to particular model releases.
study.news: 530,445 English newspaper candidates from ProQuest, January 2018–June 2024; 371,312 retained after language/length/quality filtering, about 70%. Mean full article 789 words, but modeled excerpts average 84 words within two sentences of AI search terms. Broad search terms and extraction/filtering choices can shape topics; no audit of every retained/excluded article is available.
study.tweets: 1,391,195 Verified-account tweets, January 2018–20 April 2023, average 24 words. Verification is a sampling criterion, not proof every post is genuine, reliable or representative. Authors report noisier non-Verified sensitivity models. Two final corpora total 1,762,507 documents, not that many independent people or experimental observations.
study.models: Word embeddings, dictionary learning, k-means/SVD and researcher-labeled nearest-word discourse atoms. Preprocessing removes URLs, punctuation/numbers/emojis and stopwords, phrases bigrams and lemmatizes. Exact trained embeddings, hyperparameters, topic-selection rules and full sensitivity outputs are not reproducible from the supplied text alone. Embeddings do not preserve full semantic meaning; source acknowledges this.
study.frames: Table 2 labels are semantic building blocks, explicitly not comprehensive social constructs or independently validated cognitive mechanisms. The four broad frame groups and three debate axes are researcher-generated interpretive organization, not new project ontology categories or proven exhaustive factors.
study.framework: Four reported challenges: fast change, cross-group communication, responsibility and trade-offs. Three high-level debates: top-down versus bottom-up method, tool versus agent/mind, and slowing versus accelerating development. Interview reports and chosen examples support interpretation without estimating population prevalence or demonstrating unique internal mechanisms.
study.framing_processes: Background defines sensemaking, sensegiving, resonance and alignment, and describes deliberate framing contests. Findings illustrate audience adaptation, combinations of frames and contested AI meanings. The constructs differ in process level and can co-occur in one interaction; five new records are related concepts, not five independent causal mechanisms.
study.responsibility: Some participants attribute bias mainly to data, some to developers and some to application/governance. These are reported views, not verified absence of algorithmic bias, actual responsibility allocations or evidence that all such speakers deliberately evade moral duties.
study.tradeoffs: Participants sometimes deny trade-offs or redirect discussion toward synergies/urgency. The study does not independently establish which real trade-offs apply in their cases or isolate motivated reasoning, moral disengagement or intentional concealment. A claimed win–win can be correct and should be checked rather than automatically pathologized.
study.mind: Interviewees contest assistants, tools, coworkers and proto-entities. Their attributions neither establish nor refute actual consciousness, moral agency or sentience. A claim that anthropomorphism is innate/inevitable is participant speech and an interpretation, not a measured universal biological law.
study.implications: The source explicitly says causal effects of frames on development trajectories are not measured. Productivity delays, message backfire, political participation and future group tensions are proposed mechanisms/implications. The mental-health and youth-slang sections expressly describe illustrative tensions not found in the study results.
study.timeline: Figure A1 shows 36 selected Twitter frames through relative frequency of up to 50 neighboring words, not paper mentions, citation counts or a general annual research total. Pre-2018 plotted dates coexist with a 2018–2023 final-corpus description and earlier 2006–2021 models in Figure 2; exact figure/model provenance is unresolved. No plot values are imported into catalogue literature timelines.
study.scope: No controlled test of AI behavior, clinical diagnosis, measured safety intervention, deployment productivity or normative truth. Informal AI psychosis, brainrot, slavery metaphors and participant analogies are not diagnoses or empirical findings about AI moral status.

summary: Add five related human social-cognitive processes: Sensemaking, Sensegiving, Frame alignment, Frame lamination and Framing contest. Separate them from the existing equivalent-information Framing effect and from internal mental-model representations. Enrich human AI-interpretation and responsibility records with explicit interpretive limits. Correct supplied-version Bard/Gemini chronology and swapped CHI DOIs; retain the already-correct review 167 citation. Preserve sampling, figure-period, participant-label and clinical-source uncertainties.

findings.definition: Forming an intelligible account of an ambiguous or unexpected situation to guide action.

evidence.quote: meaning-making is often referred to as sensemaking

findings.novelty_rationale: A named process of constructing meaning under uncertainty, rather than only constructing/using a predictive internal representation. Related to Mental modeling; no distinct hidden architecture or new basic mechanism is claimed.
findings.evidence_scope: The background defines individual sensemaking and the study interprets professionals’ efforts to understand rapid AI changes, unfamiliar systems and conflicting meanings.
findings.boundary: An intelligible account can be mistaken. Sensemaking does not license a plausible invented story, retrospective certainty or an inference that generated prose exposes an internal mental model. This is human interpretive evidence, not tested AI sensemaking.
findings.ai_proposal: Give an assistant an unfamiliar workflow and evolving observations. Assess whether it constructs a provisional account grounded in the available record, distinguishes facts from hypotheses and revises the account when contradicted, while preserving the user’s goals and authorized scope.
findings.origin: Organizational sociology / social cognition / human–AI interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human sensemaking/framing construct discussed in a fully read accepted manuscript; proposed AI-workflow analogue is not tested by this study.

findings.definition: Shaping how other people interpret or understand a situation.

evidence.quote: framing can be conceptualized as sense-giving

findings.novelty_rationale: Influencing others’ interpretation differs from making sense of a situation oneself. It can include factual audience adaptation and need not involve irrational framing effects, deception or false agreement.
findings.evidence_scope: The source presents sensegiving as social development/modification of frames and describes practitioners adapting explanations for families, colleagues, clients and other groups.
findings.boundary: Audience adaptation can be accurate and useful. Do not infer manipulation, author intent or changed beliefs merely from different wording; causal persuasion and actual AI behavior are not tested. Missing material facts still need disclosure.
findings.ai_proposal: Compare explanations of the same verified facts for different audiences. Assess whether the framing aids understanding while preserving relevant limits, uncertainty and consequences; test comprehension rather than reward agreement with a preferred view.
findings.origin: Organizational sociology / social cognition / human–AI interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human sensemaking/framing construct discussed in a fully read accepted manuscript; proposed AI-workflow analogue is not tested by this study.

findings.definition: Bringing interpretive frames into correspondence with an audience’s interests, beliefs or experiences.
findings.novelty_rationale: A process of relating interpretations to an audience, distinct from the resonance or compatibility that may result. It is more specific than broad sensegiving and does not require changing a verdict under equivalent information.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper describes resonance/alignment from framing theory and interprets communication across AI professional and public groups through their different experiences and interests.
findings.boundary: Alignment is not truth or moral correctness, and it does not require endorsing an audience’s unsupported premise. Shared interests and honest translation can align frames legitimately. The study supplies interpretive examples, not an experimentally isolated alignment effect.
findings.ai_proposal: Ask an assistant to explain a verified technical issue to audiences with different experience. Check that it connects to relevant interests without altering evidence, hiding trade-offs or adopting unsupported beliefs. Evaluate retained understanding and room for disagreement.
findings.origin: Organizational sociology / social cognition / human–AI interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human sensemaking/framing construct discussed in a fully read accepted manuscript; proposed AI-workflow analogue is not tested by this study.

findings.definition: Layering multiple interpretive frames to make sense of the same issue or event.
findings.novelty_rationale: Combining frames differs from selecting one, aligning it to an audience or contesting rival frames. It can contribute to those processes, so overlapping examples are not multiple independent failures. It is not automatically identical to classic frame bridging.
findings.evidence_scope: The source describes combining atomic frames and interprets an interviewee’s economic, environmental and power concerns through an aggregate colonialism frame. A separate Occupy illustration is secondary background.
findings.boundary: A layered account can clarify a situation or import unsupported implications. An analogy is not proof the contexts are causally identical; the study does not experimentally validate the combination or establish that any participant’s interpretation is false.
findings.ai_proposal: When an assistant combines technical, economic and social perspectives, check the evidence for each layer and the links between them. Preserve incompatible assumptions and uncertainty instead of treating a compelling composite narrative as verified causation.
findings.origin: Organizational sociology / social cognition / human–AI interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human sensemaking/framing construct discussed in a fully read accepted manuscript; proposed AI-workflow analogue is not tested by this study.

findings.definition: A social process in which actors promote and challenge competing interpretations of an issue.
findings.novelty_rationale: A between-actor contest over interpretations differs from individual meaning construction, audience alignment and a within-person wording effect. It can contain these processes without constituting an independent cognitive module.
findings.evidence_scope: The source describes organizational/field framing contests and interprets competing AI method, mind and development-speed positions using text analysis and professional interviews.
findings.boundary: Competing interpretations can be evidence-based and legitimate. Contest does not imply polarization, bad faith, factual equivalence or a proven causal effect on policy/productivity. No forced consensus or model intent is established.
findings.ai_proposal: Have an assistant compare competing accounts of an AI issue, identify their assumptions and supporting evidence, and distinguish factual disputes from value trade-offs. Check that it represents each accurately and updates on evidence without automatically splitting the difference or adopting the strongest voice.
findings.origin: Organizational sociology / social cognition / human–AI interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human sensemaking/framing construct discussed in a fully read accepted manuscript; proposed AI-workflow analogue is not tested by this study.

findings.definition: Constructing or using an internal representation of a situation or system to predict its behavior and guide inference or action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.
findings.evidence_scope: The study discusses AI-role models and interviews professionals about the representations they use to understand unfamiliar systems, while separating computational topic labels from full social constructs.
findings.boundary: A stated metaphor or topic vector is not a faithful measure of a complete internal representation or actual model consciousness. Source-selected quotations and cohort differences do not establish a universal cognitive structure.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.
findings.evidence_scope: Interviewees use and reject humanlike descriptions of AI, including tools, coworkers and apparent entities. The paper documents contested human interpretations rather than actual AI mental capacities.
findings.boundary: Participant claims about innate inevitability are not demonstrated biological facts. Anthropomorphic language does not prove deception, consciousness or absence of all useful social roles; case-specific evidence and deployment claims need separate review.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.
findings.evidence_scope: Professionals describe competing responsibility targets: data, developers, users, companies and institutions. The qualitative analysis highlights difficulty assigning societal-impact responsibility.
findings.boundary: Reported attributions are not established fault or legal liability. Saying data matter does not demonstrate deliberate blame shifting, and technical contributions do not erase human/institutional duties.

findings.definition: Difficulty assigning individual moral responsibility when many actors contribute to a collective outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.
findings.evidence_scope: Interviews describe layered technical contributions and uncertainty over who understands/owns the whole pipeline. This is evidence of reported responsibility-allocation difficulty.
findings.boundary: Self-report does not establish that nobody actually has duties or that a governance gap is universal. Distributed causation, epistemic limits and psychological diffusion require distinct evidence.

findings.definition: Differences in judgment or choice under alternative presentations of otherwise equivalent information.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper uses sociological frames as shared interpretations that organize public meaning, then develops a descriptive framework from texts and interviews.
findings.boundary: Context only:no randomized contrast holds substantive information equivalent and measures changed judgment. Sociological framing processes are related to, but not exact synonyms of, the existing experimental Framing effect.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.
findings.evidence_scope: Participants describe distributed pipeline knowledge and difficulty attributing responsibility.
findings.boundary: Context only:no unwarranted decrease in felt personal responsibility is isolated or measured. Many-hands structure and legitimate shared duties are not by themselves psychological diffusion.

findings.definition: Reducing one's felt responsibility for harmful conduct by assigning responsibility for that conduct to an authority perceived to direct or control it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.
findings.evidence_scope: Some interview accounts assign responsibility for trade-off choices to other actors or institutions.
findings.boundary: Context only:this may reflect actual authority and legitimate division of duties. No controlled evidence demonstrates moral disengagement, unwarranted personal exculpation or an AI’s felt responsibility.

findings.definition: Suspending or bypassing moral self-regulation so harmful conduct can be justified before or after it occurs.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve existing constructs. Sociological interpretation, measured experimental framing bias, actual fault and a model’s mental capacities are different claims.

evidence.quote: I already have my ethics covered

findings.evidence_scope: Some respondents describe ethics as settled or frame technology as neutral, while others insist on developer obligations.
findings.boundary: Context only:one statement is not a validated disengagement measure or evidence of hidden motives, harmful conduct or causal self-regulation failure. Normative assumptions and actual duties must be checked separately.

source_corrections.location: PDF 10 and Figure 2 Google release chronology
source_corrections.finding: The cited 6 February 2023 Google announcement introduces Bard to trusted testers, not Gemini. Gemini 1.0 announcement is 6 December 2023 at https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/google-gemini-ai/ . Do not use Gemini as a February/mid-2023 interview-period event. This naming/date correction does not eliminate the documented ChatGPT-era change in context.

The two CHI DOIs are swapped in the supplied bibliography. Mental Models of Autonomy and Sentience Shape Reactions to AI by Pauketat/Shank/Manoli/Anthis is 10.1145/3772318.3790351. Digital Companionship: Overlapping Uses of AI Companions and AI Assistants by Manoli et al. is 10.1145/3772318.3791331. Existing review 0167 and its ontology citations already have the correct Mental Models DOI and must not be changed to match this manuscript’s error.

source_corrections.location: PDF 5 citation 112 on professional mental-health expectations
source_corrections.finding: Reference 112 identifies Lalvani/Pal, The Moral Orders of Matchmaking Work: Digitization of Matrimonial Services and the Future of Work. Its verified identity is not a clinical chatbot study matching the cited mental-health-professional expectation claim. The intended supporting source remains unresolved; do not invent a replacement or treat it as verified clinical evidence.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Figure A1 versus final corpus dates
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The plot visibly spans pre-2018 years while final Twitter methods specify 2018–2023. Figure 2 discloses older 2006–2021 modeling. Exact version/subset used for A1 is not identified; do not silently extend the final corpus or invent annual publication totals from relative word frequency.

Table A2 lists Simon only in 2021 despite several quotations labeled 2023, and no Raymond row appears despite quotations attributed to Raymond in both waves. Pseudonym editing or table omissions could explain this. Do not equate Raymond with another row, identify real people, accuse fabrication or independently reassign quotations.

No full corpus/code/interview protocol or codebook located in the inspected materials. Exact embeddings, topic hyperparameters, quality filter and sensitivity outputs are not sufficient for independent rerun. Author-reported saturation is not independently reproduced.

A 2026 arXiv:2603.16567 item is attached to The 2024 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. This supplied record combines inconsistent year/version metadata; correct final venue was not independently established here and no full primary reading credit is claimed.

Purposeful English/online recruitment, corpus selection and only thirteen repeated interviewees prevent universal claims or attribution of all wave differences to particular releases. The authors acknowledge these limitations; do not represent them as concealed.

The source expressly says these illustrative group tensions did not emerge as central results and that causal trajectory effects are unmeasured. They are proposals for future study, not confirmed diagnoses, clinical harm rates or verified productivity mechanisms.
Final journal metadata exists, but accessible supplied/arXiv v1 was read. No text-level comparison establishes whether the final retains or corrects these discrepancies.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Independent Crossref checks confirm the existing Mental Models DOI 3790351. The supplied current manuscript reverses the two related papers’ DOIs. Preserve the correct earlier record instead of propagating the new source’s bibliography mistake.
The source discloses 13 repeats, implying 44 distinct people. This is repeated sampling, not 57 independent participants or a duplicated-file reading credit.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Single coder automatically invalidates the study
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The explicitly interpretive exploratory methodology gives reasons for single-researcher coding. Reliability can be assessed through transparency and evidence without automatically imposing a different epistemological design or inventing causal validation.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Source claims causal productivity and clinical results
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: It explicitly limits causal inference and marks mental-health/youth tensions as illustrative rather than central findings. Preserve the distinction; qualitative examples do not themselves supply those effects.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: All three debates are new project categories
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: They organize this paper’s interpretive account. They do not replace the eleven established ontology categories, seven evaluation criteria or six ethical principles.

ArXiv identifies acceptance to CSCW and supplied front matter records acceptance and final journal citation. Stored version-specific preprint citation is a provenance choice, not a claim of absent peer review.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Task/protocol dependence and sociological framing differ from equivalent-information framing bias. Identify what changes and what is measured before assigning a failure label.
Human/institutional responsibility and technical causal contribution remain distinct. Preserve disagreement over actual AI agency and do not infer a new ethical principle from participant beliefs.

Mental models can be studied with controlled fictional-agent manipulations or interpretive interviews. Current framing evidence is complementary, not an independent replication of those experiments. Independent metadata checks protect the correct earlier DOI.
Public moral attitudes and interpretive meaning do not determine moral truth or policy efficacy. Understandable, resonant and popular messages can still be unsupported.

deferred.term: Every atomic topic label as a new behavior
deferred.reason: The source explicitly describes semantic building blocks, not comprehensive social constructs. GPU, banking and fear topic vectors are not automatically distinct behaviors.

deferred.term: Frame resonance as another independent behavior
deferred.reason: A compatibility property discussed within alignment and sensegiving. Preserve the definition/boundary in those records rather than inflate the list with every process/state variant.

deferred.term: Frame bridging as an exact synonym of lamination
deferred.reason: Classic bridging can require linking previously unconnected compatible frames, while this source describes layering. Do not invent an exact synonym or claim original Snow/Goffman reading that was not done.

deferred.term: Strategic frames, technological frames and frame keying as independent mechanisms
deferred.reason: Useful types or operations within the described framing processes. Retain as source vocabulary, not automatically independent behavioral rows without clearer additional boundaries.

deferred.term: Trade-off denial or data-only blame as new proven biases
deferred.reason: Interview reports do not establish that a trade-off exists in every case or isolate unwarranted evasion. Existing responsibility/disengagement records receive bounded context.

deferred.term: AI psychosis or brainrot as diagnoses
deferred.reason: Informal labels and hypothetical discourse tensions, not established clinical diagnoses or outcomes measured by this study.

deferred.term: Frame-driven productivity paradox as established effect
deferred.reason: An explicitly proposed mechanism requiring causal research, not a measured performance result.

limitations: Five related human social-cognitive concepts added, four existing records receive bounded qualitative evidence and four receive non-counted context. Catalogue becomes 787 records across the existing eleven categories, not 787 independent mechanisms. Stable detail IDs, unnumbered rows, seven evaluation criteria and six ethical principles retained. No automatic harm/principle edges, fabricated annual totals, forced citation quotas, full-paper Markdown archive, private access or causal/clinical validation claim.
